boundary_rationale: The book's opening word is אֵיכָ֣ה (oshb:Lam.1.1, byte tier), the verse-initial cry that gives this stretch its aleph line and frames a third-person report of the ruined capital: “How the city sits solitary, that was full of people! She has become as a widow, who was great among the nations!” web:Lam.1.1. The same voice names the daughter-of-Zion formula at web:Lam.1.6 inside “All majesty has departed from the daughter of Zion.” web:Lam.1.6 (this verse also carries a ketiv/qere note per the inventory, not engaged by the present reading; the formula itself recurs seven further times book-wide, sweep: 8 verses book-wide), and keeps the same distance through the roads, gates and priests of web:Lam.1.4. The report closes on “She has no comforter.” web:Lam.1.9 immediately followed by the first-person plea “See, Yahweh, my affliction; for the enemy has magnified himself.” web:Lam.1.9, a brief intrusion of Zion's own voice inside an otherwise third-person span (a per-bytes deviation from a plain city_lament reading, disclosed rather than smoothed over). The same verse completes the contiguous refrain אֵ֥ין מְנַחֵ֖ם לָ֑הּ (oshb:Lam.1.9, byte tier; roughly "she is without a comforter"; sweep: 3 verses contiguous, byte tier), and refrains close units under the owner-ruled seam law: the boundary sits here rather than folding this verse forward with the interjection that follows it.

The report opens by naming Zion and Jacob's political ruin — “The Lord has swallowed up all the dwellings of Jacob without pity.” web:Lam.2.2 (a ketiv/qere note also marks this verse per the inventory, not engaged here), the horn of Israel cut off at web:Lam.2.3, the bent bow of web:Lam.2.4 — then turns in the same third-person voice to its cultic ruin: the tabernacle and sabbath of web:Lam.2.6, the altar and sanctuary of web:Lam.2.7, and the silent prophets of “Her gates have sunk into the ground.” web:Lam.2.9. boundary_rationale: The report's human cost gathers first in communal mourning — “The elders of the daughter of Zion sit on the ground. They keep silence.” web:Lam.2.10 — then narrows to the narrator's own body: “My eyes fail with tears. My heart is troubled.” web:Lam.2.11, where the daughter-of-my-people formula בַּת עַמִּ֑י (oshb:Lam.2.11, byte tier; sweep: 5 verses book-wide) names the destruction the narrator now feels in the first person, a voice this reading does not attempt to separate cleanly from the third-person report of the swooning children in the same verse and the next. The stretch closes on a direct turn to address: “What shall I testify to you? What shall I liken to you, daughter of Jerusalem?” web:Lam.2.13, where the virgin-daughter-of-Zion formula בְּתוּלַ֖ת בַּת צִיּ֑וֹן (oshb:Lam.2.13, byte tier; sweep: 2 verses book-wide) and the daughter-of-Jerusalem phrase הַבַּת֙ יְר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם (oshb:Lam.2.13, byte tier) both sit inside one rhetorical question. Where exactly the narrator's own first person gives way to this address — at web:Lam.2.11 itself, or once the vocative names its addressee at web:Lam.2.13 — is held open rather than decided here.

boundary_rationale: The report turns to direct imperative address: “Their heart cried to the Lord. O wall of the daughter of Zion, let tears run down like a river day and night.” web:Lam.2.18 and “Arise, cry out in the night, at the beginning of the watches!” web:Lam.2.19 (a ketiv/qere note also marks this second verse per the inventory, not engaged by the present reading).
